wiki.extract: Grand Anse Beach is Grenada's most famous beach, a two-mile crescent of white sand and calm turquoise water just south of St. George's. Lined with resorts and restaurants, it is the center of the island's tourism industry.

The Molinere Underwater Sculpture Park, off Grenada's west coast, is the world's first underwater sculpture gallery, created by Jason deCaires Taylor in 2006. Its submerged statues, which double as artificial reefs, make it one of the Caribbean's most celebrated dive and snorkel sites.

Fort George, perched on a promontory above St. George's harbor, is an 18th-century French-built fortress later used by the British. It offers sweeping views of the capital and is a landmark of Grenada's colonial and revolutionary history.

The Grenada National Museum, housed in a former French barracks in St. George's, traces the island's history from Amerindian settlement through slavery, colonialism, and the 1979-83 revolution. Its exhibits include artifacts from the revolutionary era.

Carriacou, the largest of Grenada's sister islands, is known for its boatbuilding tradition, pristine beaches, and vibrant parang and carnival festivals. Its main town, Hillsborough, preserves a quiet, traditional Caribbean character.

Spicemas is Grenada's national carnival, held each August with soca and calypso music, J'ouvert dawn parades, and the Monday Night Mas and Pretty Mas street parades in St. George's. Nicknamed for Grenada's spice heritage, it is the island's biggest cultural celebration.

The Carriacou Parang Festival is an annual December celebration of parang, the traditional Christmas string-band music of the southern Caribbean. Bands compete with guitars, cuatros, and maracas in a festive, community-rooted atmosphere on Carriacou.

Carriacou holds its own traditional carnival each February, a smaller and more community-rooted celebration than Grenada's Spicemas. It features street parades, calypso, and the island's distinctive cultural traditions.

The Grenada Chocolate Festival is an annual May celebration of the island's fine-flavour Trinitario cocoa, with estate tours, tree-to-bar workshops, tastings, and chocolate-inspired food, art, and wellness events. Launched in 2014, it showcases Grenada's bean-to-bar chocolate makers.

Grenada marks its independence from Britain every February 7, commemorating the 1974 achievement with official ceremonies, military parades, and cultural performances nationwide. It is the country's principal patriotic holiday.

food_writeup: Grenadian cuisine reflects the island's 'Spice Isle' identity, built on nutmeg, cinnamon, and cocoa; the national dish is oil down, a slow-cooked one-pot of breadfruit, callaloo, coconut milk, and salted meat. Fresh seafood, lambi (conch), and cocoa tea are staples, and the island's chocolate and rum are prized exports.
brief_history: Grenada was colonized by the French and then the British, who built a plantation economy on enslaved African labor and made the island a leading nutmeg producer. After independence in 1974, the 1979 revolution led by Maurice Bishop ended with his 1983 assassination and a U.S.-led intervention; since then Grenada has been a stable parliamentary democracy known for spices, tourism, and Olympic champion Kirani James.
current_conflicts: Grenada has no active armed conflict or internal insurgency. Its main security concerns are small-island issues such as drug transshipment, alongside the long recovery from Hurricane Beryl's 2024 devastation of Carriacou and Petite Martinique.
